newsitem.title: USA: Bob Dole gets election drive boost from George Bush.
newsitem.headline: Bob Dole gets election drive boost from George Bush.

text.p: Former President George Bush pitched in on Thursday to give underdog Republican presidential challenger Bob Dole a helping hand in his uphill struggle, accusing President Bill Clinton of using the White House for partisan politics.
"I believe in keeping the White House above partisan politics and away from these puny disputes we're seeing," Bush, who was beaten by Clinton in 1992, said at a rally.

In accusing Clinton of running a partisan White House, Bush implicitly referred to brewing controversies over donations to the Democratic Party from people with ties to Indonesia, Taiwan and other foreign interests.
"I want to be known as a loyal friend of Bob Dole, a Bob Dole admirer," Bush said in introducing his rival for the 1988 Republican presidential nomination.
"Bob Dole is the person to lead this country into the next millenium. What it's about is leadership. ... We need somebody to restore the respect to America around the world."
In his remarks at the Tampa Theatre rally, Dole said he was gaining on the Democratic incumbent. "Five big days left and the polls are going to close on Nov. 5," Dole said.
"As you know today is Halloween. All the kids are dressing up and doing scary things," Dole said. "You know, that's the way it is every day at the Clinton White House."

The former senator continued hammering Clinton on what he said was a "disastrous" economy and a "mediscare' campaign he said was frightening senior citizens who make up a large portion of the Florida population.

He said it was "irresponsible" to suggest a Dole White House would cut the popular Medicare health programme for older people. "I was the senator who helped save and strengthen Social Security. And I will be the president who saves and strengthens medicare."

He said he would name a bipartisan commission to preserve Medicare and announced he would name Democratic New York Sen. Pat Moynihan and Republican Florida Sen. Connie Mack as the first two appointments to the panel.
Dole, Bush and Mrs. Dole appeared on the same stage at the theatre. While Dole and Bush have appeared together before, this was the first time at a campaign rally.

The Doles will head to Miami for a rally underscoring the importance of this state, which Bush carried in his loss to Clinton four years ago. Dole then campaigns in another Southern state, Georgia, which went for Clinton four years ago, before going to Ohio, also a key state.
Florida, which has been voting Republican in recent presidential elections, is the fourth largest state and has 25 of the 270 electoral votes needed to win the election.

The independent Florida Voter Poll, published by the Miami Herald on Tuesday, showed 47 percent of the state's voters favoured Clinton compared to 39 percent for Dole, eight percent for Reform Party candidate Ross Perot and 6 percent undecided.
Nationally, Clinton holds a much larger lead, in double digits in some surveys. If Dole wins, he would have come from farther behind than any winner in the history of modern polling.

At a rally in a New Orleans suburb on Wednesday night, Dole reminded his audience that Democrat Harry Truman came from way behind to defeat Republican Tom Dewey in 1948, a victory remembered by the photo of Truman holding up a copy of the Chicago Tribune with a large headline "Dewey Wins."
"Keep your eye on me -- I'm going to be a second Harry Truman," he shouted to wild applause.
